title: Go Tell the Craftsman
summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon comes home proud from the house of study and says hurtful words about the looks of a man he meets on the road. The man's answer, "Go tell the Craftsman who made me," makes him see his mistake and ask forgiveness. A story about respect for every person, and the courage to admit a wrong and say sorry.
pages: Rabbi Elazar, the son of Rabbi Shimon, was coming home from his teacher's house. He rode a donkey along the riverbank, and the water flowed quietly beside him. His heart was full of joy, because he had learned a great deal of Torah. But he also felt very important – maybe a little too important.
On the way he met a man. The man looked very different from all the people Rabbi Elazar knew; his face was not like other people's faces. The man smiled and said politely, "Peace be with you, Rabbi!"

But Rabbi Elazar did not answer his greeting. Instead, he said hurtful words about the way the man looked, and even asked whether all the people in his town looked like him. The words flew out fast, like arrows. And the man stood there, and his face grew sad.

The man answered quietly, "I do not know. But go and tell the Craftsman who made me."
That meant: "I did not choose how I look. The One who created me is the Holy One, blessed be He – the great Craftsman. If you have complaints about how I look, go and tell them to Him."

Suddenly Rabbi Elazar understood what he had done, and his heart ached. He hurried down from the donkey, bowed low before the man and said, "I was wrong, forgive me!" – meaning: "You are right, I admit it. Please, forgive me!" But the man was very hurt. "I will not forgive you," he said, "until you go to the Craftsman who made me and tell Him what you told me."

The man kept walking toward his town, and Rabbi Elazar followed him all the way, on foot, with his head bowed. When they reached the town, the townspeople came out joyfully to greet Rabbi Elazar: "Peace be with you, Rabbi, Rabbi! Our teacher, our teacher!" They were so happy that a great sage had come to them.

The man asked them, "Who are you calling 'Rabbi, Rabbi'?"
"The one walking behind you," they answered.
"If this is a rabbi," said the man, "may there not be many like him in Israel!" And he told them what had happened on the road. The townspeople begged him, "Please, forgive him. He is a man great in Torah."

The man thought for a moment, and then said, "For your sake I forgive him – as long as he does not make a habit of it." That meant: as long as he never hurts anyone like that, ever again. Rabbi Elazar thanked him with all his heart. And from that day on, he changed.

That same day Rabbi Elazar went into the house of study and taught: "A person should always be soft like a reed, and not hard like a cedar." A reed is a thin, bendy plant that bends in the wind. A cedar is a tall, hard tree. That means: it is better to be soft and gentle, to know how to bend and say sorry – and not to be hard and proud.

Each one of us was made differently: tall or short, with glasses or freckles, with curly hair or straight. And the same great Craftsman made all of us, with love. That is why we never laugh at how someone looks. And if we do hurt someone anyway – it happens – we can do what Rabbi Elazar did: stop, admit it, and say sorry.
